ca-a-igloo.s: An igloo is a house made of snow bricks. The Inuit, a people of the north, cut thick blocks of snow and lay them in a circle, and each new row leans a little closer to the middle. It makes a spiral, and at the end a round roof, a dome. The gaps are filled with snow. Snow is full of air, and air keeps the warmth in. So inside an igloo, even in a hard frost, it is much warmer than outside. Long ago, hunters could build one in a couple of hours when they needed a place to sleep on a journey.

ca-a-inuksuk.s: In the northern tundra, where there are no trees and no fences, you suddenly see a little man made of stones. It is an inuksuk. It is built from big stones: legs, a body, and sometimes arms. The word means something like “standing in for a person”. Inuksuit show travellers the way, tell them where the good fishing places are, and help hunters. If you see one, it means people have been here before. A stone man like this was also drawn on the badge of the 2010 Winter Olympic Games.

ca-a-parka.s: The whole world knows the word “parka”, but it was the northern peoples who invented this kind of coat. Long ago, parkas were sewn from caribou skins: a caribou’s fur is hollow inside and keeps in the warmth better than many cloths. Inuit mums had a special parka called an amauti. It has a big hood at the back where the baby sat. It is as warm as a little nest in there, and Mum’s hands are free. Needles were made from bones and thread from sinews. The sewing was beautiful, with patterns.
a: In a pocket on the sleeve

ca-a-narwhal.s: In the cold waters of the Arctic lives the narwhal, a kind of whale. It has a long twisted tusk sticking out, like the unicorn in fairy tales. In fact it is a tooth, and it grows right out of the upper jaw, most often on the left. It can be up to three metres long. Long ago, people thought such tusks came from magic animals, and they sold them as unicorn horns. Narwhals live in groups, love the cold and dive very deep. Their skin is spotted, grey and white.

ca-b-rideau.s: In Canada’s capital, Ottawa, there is a canal called the Rideau Canal. In summer, boats sail on it, but in winter the water freezes and the canal turns into a huge skating rink! It stretches for almost eight kilometres. People skate to work and to school, and then drink hot chocolate at stalls right on the ice. According to the Guinness Book of Records, it is the biggest natural ice rink in the world, because the winter itself freezes the ice.
a: It freezes and becomes a skating rink
It goes off to warm countries
It fills up with hot cocoa

ca-b-orcas.s: Not far from Vancouver, orcas live in the sea. They are not fish, they are big dolphins! Orcas swim in families, and the boss of a family is usually the grandmother. The babies stay close to their mum for many years. The families talk to each other with clicks and whistles, and each one has its own “accent”. People go out in boats to watch orcas, but they do not go close, so as not to scare them. And if it is raining in Vancouver, which it often is, people simply put on their raincoats.
a: A seagull sitting on its back

ca-b-fundy.s: The Bay of Fundy in eastern Canada has the highest tides in the world. Twice a day the sea rises and falls, and at the biggest tides the water changes by as much as sixteen metres. That is like a five-storey house! At low tide, boats lie right on the bottom, on the wet sand, and you can walk on the seabed. Then the water comes back, and the boats float again. In one tide, billions of tonnes of water flow into the bay.
a: They lie on the bottom, on the sand
They fly off into the clouds

ca-b-banff-bridges.s: In Banff National Park, in the Rocky Mountains, bridges and tunnels were built across a big road, but not for people, for animals. There are six bridges and thirty-eight tunnels. The bridges are covered in grass and trees, so they look like woodland clearings. Deer, mountain sheep and even grizzly bears cross over them. This way the animals go wherever they like, and the cars drive along calmly without scaring anyone.

ca-b-naismith.s: Basketball was invented by a Canadian, James Naismith. In 1891 he worked as a PE teacher in the USA. In winter the boys were bored in the gym, and he needed a new game. He hung two peach baskets on the balcony, took a football and wrote thirteen rules. The baskets hung about three metres high, and today the hoop in basketball hangs at the same height.

ca-b-poutine.s: In Quebec, people invented a dish with a funny name: poutine (say “poo-TEEN”). It is hot chips, with pieces of fresh young cheese on top, and then it is all covered with warm gravy. The cheese in poutine is special: while it is fresh, it squeaks on your teeth! The dish began in the villages of Quebec, and now it is eaten all over Canada. Grown-ups say poutine is best when it is cold outside.

cas-b-delfiny.s: Boats set off from Cascais to look for dolphins. The dolphins live in the ocean not far from the shore. They love to swim right beside the front of a boat, jumping out of the water. Every dolphin has its own special whistle, a bit like our names. When friends hear it, they know who is calling. You do not see dolphins every day, so everyone on the boat watches the waves and waits for a grey back to flash by.
a: By the smell of a tail

cas-b-osminog.s: Octopuses hide among the rocks along the coast of Portugal. They have eight arms and three whole hearts! Two send blood to the gills, and one sends it round the whole body. An octopus has bluish blood. It is very clever: it can open jars, find its way, and change colour to blend in with the stones. In the day it usually rests in its little den, and it comes out to catch crabs when it starts to get dark on the shore.

cas-c-cork.s: Cork is the bark of a special oak tree, the cork oak. Once every nine years, skilled workers carefully cut off the bark with small axes. The tree does not get ill, and it grows new bark. Cork is used for more than bottle stoppers: bags, purses, hats and even shoes are made from it. In the shops of Portugal, including in Cascais, you can touch light, warm cork and feel how soft it is.

cas-comboio.s: A train runs from Cascais to Lisbon, and almost all the way it goes beside the ocean. From the window you can see waves, beaches, old forts and fishing boats. The railway to Cascais opened in 1889. Then people from Lisbon began to take the train to the seaside to swim and to walk. Later, some of the first electric trains in Portugal ran here.

cas-cresmina.s: Next to Guincho beach lies the Cresmina dune, a big hill of sand. But this hill does not stay still! The strong wind blows and blows, and carries the sand grain by grain. In one year the dune moves about the length of a bus. To keep from stepping on the plants, people walk on wooden paths. From there you can see the wind drawing little waves in the sand.

cas-lota.s: When the fishermen of Cascais come back from the sea, they bring their catch to the lota. The lota is a fish auction, where fish is sold by special rules. The boxes of fish are shown one by one. First the price is high, and then it gets lower and lower. The buyer who gives a sign first takes the box. This way fresh fish quickly gets to the shops and restaurants.
a: It flies up to the moon
It jumps back into the sea

cas-fleming.s: In Estoril, next to Cascais, there is a casino. It is a big, fancy building where grown-ups play cards and other games. In front of it is a garden with palm trees. A long time ago, the English writer Ian Fleming stayed in Estoril and watched people play in the casino. They say the Estoril casino helped him to think up the first book about the brave spy James Bond. A spy is a secret agent, and many films were made about James Bond later.

cas-b-sardina-na-hlebe.s: In summer, the seaside in Portugal smells of smoke, because sardines are grilled over hot coals. They do not need a plate. The hot little fish is laid right on a slice of bread. The bread soaks up the juice and becomes the tastiest bit. Sardines live in big shoals and swim shoulder to shoulder, as if they were marching. The fishermen of Cascais catch them in nets, and then they grill them on the shore for everyone.

cas-b-olushi.s: In winter, big white birds with black wing tips fly over the ocean near Portugal. They are gannets. When a gannet spots a fish, it folds its wings and drops like an arrow, from as high as a tall block of flats. It hits the water as fast as a car on a motorway. So that its head does not hurt, it has little air cushions under its skin. Then the gannet pops up with a fish in its beak.
a: It drops into the water like an arrow
It digs with its feet in the sand

cas-b-kajtsurf.s: Guincho beach, not far from Cascais, is loved by everyone who needs wind. In the sky above the waves float huge, bright kites, striped, green and yellow. Under each one stands a person on a board, a kitesurfer. The wind fills the kite and pulls it forward, and the board along the water with it. The kitesurfer can even jump over the waves like a grasshopper. The whole beach looks up and laughs with joy.

cas-c-santini-ice-cream.s: In 1949, an Italian man called Attilio Santini opened a little ice cream shop on Tamariz beach, near Cascais. Later, another shop like it opened in Cascais itself. People liked the ice cream so much that on hot days there is a queue at the counter. The family says they still make it from the same recipes as many years ago. And there are so many flavours that your eyes go wide: chocolate, berries, lemon.

cas-b-luzhi-na-kamnyah.s: When the ocean goes out, little pools are left between the rocks. For a crab, it is a whole home! Take a look into one. Sea anemones that look like flowers sit there, a starfish creeps along, and tiny fish dart about. They are all waiting for the water to come back. Look at them gently, do not pull them out, and put the stones back, because under them is somebody’s bedroom. The best time to hunt for wonders is just after the tide goes out.

cas-c-calceteiro.s: The pavements of Cascais are laid by hand. The pavement maker crouches down with a little hammer and picks up small stones: white ones of limestone and black ones of basalt. He sets them into the sand one by one and taps them until each stone sits flat. This is how patterns appear in the squares: waves, fish, ships and stars. The work is slow, but you can walk on these pictures as much as you like.

cas-paula-rego.s: In Cascais there is a museum with two red towers. The towers are pointed, like pyramids, and you can see them from far away above the trees. It is the House of Stories of the painter Paula Rego. Paula Rego painted pictures like fairy tales, about girls, dogs and other animals. You can look at each picture for a long time and imagine what will happen next.

cas-castro-guimaraes.s: In Cascais, above a little bay, there is a house like a fairy-tale castle with a small tower. It was built more than a hundred years ago. Later, Count Castro Guimarães lived in it. He collected old things and books. The count left his castle-house to the town, and now it is a museum. The museum keeps a book that is more than five hundred years old, and in it is one of the oldest drawings of Lisbon.

cas-praia-rainha.s: Right in the middle of Cascais, a tiny beach hides between the rocks. It is called Praia da Rainha, which means “the Queen’s Beach”. A long time ago, Queen Amélia swam here. She was the wife of King Carlos. In those days this beach was only for her. Now everyone can swim here, and children build sandcastles where the queen once swam.

cas-rei-carlos.s: King Carlos the First loved the sea very much. On the yacht “Amélia”, named after the queen, he sailed out into the ocean near Cascais. The king let his nets down deep, deep down and pulled up fish and other sea creatures to study them. He could also paint the sea beautifully. Now Cascais has a Museum of the Sea, named after King Carlos.

cas-oitavos.s: On the shore of the ocean, not far from Cascais, stands the old Oitavos fortress. It was built almost four hundred years ago to guard the coast. Day and night, soldiers watched the sea to see if strange ships were sailing near. Now the fortress is a museum, and anyone can go in. You can stand by the old wall and watch the waves, like a real sentry.

cas-cabo-raso.s: On the road from Cascais to Guincho beach, there is a rocky point called Cabo Raso. A little lighthouse stands on it, as red as a fire engine. It was built right inside an old fortress, behind its walls. The lighthouse has shone for ships for more than a hundred years, and its light can be seen far out at sea. In the old days a keeper looked after the light, but now the lighthouse switches itself on.

cas-carcavelos.s: Carcavelos is a long sandy beach between Cascais and Lisbon. Surfers with long boards come here all year round. The water in the ocean is chilly, so they wear wetsuits that look like rubber skin. A surfer lies on the board, paddles with their hands like a duck with its feet, catches a wave and stands up. The wave carries them to the shore, as if down a slide! On the beach there are surf schools where even children learn.

cas-mercado.s: In the middle of Cascais there is a market called Mercado da Vila. Early in the morning, farmers from the villages around bring vegetables, fruit, bread, cheese and flowers. In the fish row, silvery fish shine on the ice, and next to them lie prawns and shells. Shoppers walk between the stalls with bags and baskets. It smells of the sea, fresh bread and oranges all at once!

cas-a-kazino-eshtoril.s: Not far from the sea, in Estoril, stands one of the biggest casinos in Europe. They began to build it in 1916, and the first stone was laid by the President of Portugal at that time. The building opened in 1931. Children do not go inside, because it is a place for grown-ups. But for travellers it has become a real landmark of Estoril: big, in a modern style, with gardens next to it that stretch down to the beach.
a: Laid the first stone of the future casino
Started the first train to Cascais
Lit the fire in a new lighthouse

cas-a-kasa-santa-mariya.s: In Cascais there is a house whose walls are decorated with azulejos, painted tiles. It is called Casa de Santa Maria. It was built in 1902, to a design by the architect Raul Lino, for a rich man called Jorge O’Neill. They say it was a wedding present for his daughter Maria Teresa. Now the house is a museum, and very close, by the sea, stands an old lighthouse that you can visit too.

cas-a-zamok-grafov.s: If you walk into the park in the middle of Cascais, you will see a little castle. It has small towers and a shady courtyard with arches, as if from a fairy tale. This is the palace of the Counts of Castro Guimarães. It was not built in ancient times, but about a hundred years ago, yet it looks like a knight’s castle. Since 1931 it has been a museum: the beautiful things the counts collected can now be looked at by everyone.
a: Small towers and a courtyard with arches
A glass dome and a fountain-hill

cas-a-park-karmona.s: Next to the counts’ castle lies the Marechal Carmona park. Ducks, hens and peacocks walk about freely here, and in the pond and on the stones by the water you can see little turtles. It is best not to feed the birds just anything, because the park looks after that. But you can sit on a bench and watch a proud peacock walk along the path as if it were his own garden.

cas-a-muzey-muzyki.s: In Monte Estoril, on a hill, there is a house-museum where music is gathered. It is the Museum of Portuguese Music. Its greatest treasure is folk instruments, collected by Michel Giacometti, who travelled around the villages and wrote down songs. The house was built in 1917–1918 for the same Jorge O’Neill, and later it became a museum and a garden for all the townspeople.

cas-a-avtodrom-eshtoril.s: Near Estoril there is a motor racing circuit, a track for races. It opened in 1972. From 1984 to 1996 the Portuguese Grand Prix was held here: the fastest racing cars in the world, Formula 1, raced round and round. Today one lap of the track is a little over four kilometres. On foot it takes almost an hour to walk it, but a racing car needs far less than two minutes.
a: A bicycle race round the country

cas-a-paredan.s: Between Cascais and Estoril, a long seaside path runs along the shore. It is called the Paredão, which in Portuguese means “big wall”. It is almost three kilometres long: exactly 2,750 metres. As you walk, the ocean splashes beside you, you can see beaches and cliffs, and you can walk from one town to the other without once turning onto a street.
a: A little less than three kilometres

cas-a-marina-kashkaysh.s: In Cascais there is a big harbour for yachts, a marina. It opened in 1999. It has 650 places for boats and yachts, and the longest yachts can be up to 36 metres, like three buses parked in a row. A hundred and twenty-five places are kept for guests who have stopped by for a couple of days: today a yacht from one country is here, tomorrow one from another.

cas-a-kubok-ameriki.s: In August 2011, the first stage of a big sailing series, the America’s Cup, took place off the coast of Cascais. Light yachts with stiff wing-like sails raced across the bay so close that people watched right from the shore. And even earlier, in 2007, Cascais hosted the World Sailing Championship. The sea here is very good for racing.

cas-a-gora-rakushek.s: Where does the town get its name, Cascais? One idea is that it is connected with shells. A long time ago, the people of this coast gathered molluscs, and an old word meant something like “mountain of shells”. Nobody knows for sure, but it is a lovely idea. Imagine: you are standing on the shore, and in front of you is a whole mountain of empty, shining shells.

cas-a-linza-mayaka.s: By the Cascais marina stands the Santa Marta lighthouse, and inside it is a museum that opened in 2007. Inside lie huge glass Fresnel lenses. One of them used to shine on the island of Berlenga and is 3 metres 70 centimetres tall, almost twice as tall as an ordinary door. Such a lens gathers the light of a lamp into one long beam, so that ships can see the lighthouse from far away.
a: Gathers the light of a lamp into a long beam
Shows what the weather will be

cas-a-doroga-marzhinal.s: A coastal road, the Marginal, leads from Lisbon to Cascais. Its name means something like “road at the edge”: it runs right along the shore. In the old days there was an ordinary dirt road in its place, and then a wide one was built, and driving along the ocean became quick and easy. Along the way, beaches, forts and houses by the water follow one after another.

cas-a-kurort-pridumali.s: About a hundred years ago, Estoril became a resort. The businessman Fausto Figueiredo and his partner began to build hotels, gardens, roads to the sea and a big casino here. A quiet place by the ocean turned into a town where guests came from many countries. Historians even call this “the invention of Estoril”, because the resort was thought up and built almost from nothing.

cas-a-vereskovoe-imya.s: Nobody knows for sure where the name Estoril comes from. Some think it came from an old word for heather, a bush with tiny flowers that grows on these hills. Others think it came from a word for a hawk. Perhaps heather bloomed on the slopes, and a hawk circled above it. Choose the idea you like better.

cas-a-rimskaya-masterskaya.s: In the middle of Cascais, the remains of a Roman workshop were found, where fish were salted. The Romans caught fish in the ocean, sprinkled them with salt so they would not go bad, and carried them away in big jars. So the people of this coast were living off the sea two thousand years ago. Today people here love fish too, only they keep it on ice and in fridges.

cas-a-derevnya-stala-gorodom.s: Once upon a time, Cascais was a fishing village. In 1364, King Pedro the First declared it a town. And in 1514, King Manuel the First gave the town a special charter: it allowed the people to decide their own town matters themselves. That made two royal gifts, and Cascais still remembers both of them.

cas-a-letnie-dachi.s: From 1870 to 1908, the royal family came to Cascais for the summer. Rich families followed and built smart summer houses by the sea. This style is called “summer architecture”. It mixes different styles, so in one house you may find a little tower, a veranda and patterned tiles. Many such houses still stand in the middle of the town.

cas-a-molodezhnaya-stolitsa.s: Every year, Europe chooses a town that is called the youth capital. In 2018, Cascais received this title. It meant that all year long the town held events for children and young people, came up with projects and listened to what young people wanted. Imagine: a whole year when a town takes care of those who are only beginning to grow.
a: The quietest town on the planet

cas-a-chetyre-eshtorila.s: You travel by train from Lisbon towards Cascais and you hear the same name many times. The stops go like this: São Pedro do Estoril, São João do Estoril, plain Estoril, Monte Estoril. Four stations in a row, and in each one there is Estoril! And after that, at the very end of the line, comes Cascais: beyond it there are no rails, only the ocean.

cas-a-plyazh-tamarish.s: Tamariz beach in Estoril begins right below the casino gardens. From the station you can walk to the sea in a few minutes, and the way goes through a green garden. They say palm trees grow there, and people walk their dogs on the lawns. Just like that: you step off the train, walk along the path, and there is hot sand under your feet.
a: To a castle on a hill

cas-a-fort-santu-antoniu.s: On the rocks near São João do Estoril stands the old fort of Santo António da Barra. It was built around 1590 so that strange ships would not come near the mouth of the Tagus river and land to get water. For many years the fort was closed, but since 2018 you can go in again: from there you can see the blue sea and the coast that it once guarded.
a: To guard the way into Lisbon from the sea

cas-a-tsepochka-fortov.s: The coast from Cascais to Lisbon looks like a chain of stone: pirates tried many times to come near here, so a whole row of forts was built along the water. After 1640, about a dozen more, smaller ones appeared. They stood so that they covered each other and the mouth of the Tagus river. They say that hardly anywhere else are there so many coastal fortresses.

cas-a-kasa-sommer.s: Casa Sommer is a big house in Cascais. It was repaired, and on 7 December 2016 its doors opened again. Inside is kept the town’s historical archive: old papers from 1387 to 2016. There is also a library and a bookshop. If you put all these sheets together, you get the history of Cascais, just as people wrote it down.

cas-a-kto-zhil-ranshe.s: People chose the Estoril coast a very long time ago. The Phoenicians were here, sailors and merchants from the east of the Mediterranean Sea, then the Romans, and then the Arabs. The remains of a Roman villa were found in Estoril. A mild climate, the sea close by and flat land: people liked all this a thousand years ago, and they like it today.

cas-a-tennis-eshtoril.s: The Portuguese tennis tournament is called the “Estoril Open”, although its first matches, in 1990, were played in the nearby town of Oeiras. Since 2015, the tournament has been held at the Estoril tennis club. Players come from all over the world with rackets and balls, and the spectators listen to the ball thumping on the court and smell the sea.
a: At an ice rink in Lisbon

cas-a-spasennye-plitki.s: In the Santa Maria house there is a chapel, and in it are tiles from the eighteenth century. They say they were saved from the ruins of an old chapel: the tiles were carefully taken down and put in a new place. These tiles show scenes from the Bible. So pictures that are almost three hundred years old found a second home, and in it they are beautiful too.
a: They were saved and put in the Santa Maria house
They were thrown into the ocean
They were sold at the market

cas-a-trassa-dlya-motociklov.s: The Estoril circuit was once for cars, and then it was changed. Around the year 2000 the track was rebuilt so that motorcyclists could race here too. Now its length is 4,183 metres. Motorcycle races were held on it for many years, and the spectators sat on the hills nearby to see the riders lean in the corners almost down to the ground.

cas-b-bakalyau.s: The Portuguese love cod very much and call it “bacalhau”. Fresh cod lives in the cold northern seas, far from Cascais. A long time ago, Portuguese fishermen sailed for it all the way to the coast of Newfoundland. So that the fish would not go bad on the way, it was salted and dried. Such cod became as hard as a board and could keep for a long, long time. At home it was soaked in water, and it came back to life for dinner.

cas-b-portugalskiy-korablik.s: After a strong wind, something blue and shiny sometimes lies on the beach, like a balloon with long strings. It is a Portuguese man o’ war. It is not a jellyfish at all, but a whole family of tiny creatures living together. On top it has an inflated bubble like a sail, and the wind pushes it over the waves. The strings under the water sting, even when it has washed up on the shore. So if you see one, do not touch it, but call a grown-up.

cas-b-baklany.s: On the dark rocks by the ocean, black birds sit, standing as if with their arms spread wide. They are cormorants. They are excellent at diving for fish, and under the water their feathers get wet. So after fishing, a cormorant climbs onto a rock, spreads its wings and dries them in the wind and sun, like washing on a line. Look how patiently it sits. It will not fly away until it is dry.

cas-b-chayki.s: On the seafront in Cascais there are always seagulls with yellow feet walking about. They are clever and watchful. A seagull likes shells and crabs, but the shell is tough, and a beak is not a pair of pliers. So it grabs its catch, flies up high and drops it onto the stones. The shell cracks, and the gull comes down for its lunch. Seagulls also remember where people eat, and keep an eye on other people’s buns. Do not leave your sandwich alone!
a: Drops it from high up onto the stones
Waits until it opens by itself

cas-b-prilivy.s: In the morning, on the beach below Cascais, there is a wide strip of wet sand, and a few hours later the water has come right up to the rocks. This happens twice a day. These are the tides, high and low. The Moon pulls the water towards it, and the huge ocean rises and falls just a little, as if it were breathing. Fishermen and surfers always check when high tide will be, so as not to be left on the rocks when the water comes.

cas-b-nortada.s: In summer, a strong wind often blows along the coast near Cascais. The Portuguese call it the nortada, from the word “norte”, which means “north”. It comes after lunch, knocks over the beach umbrellas and fills the sails. But it keeps the shore from getting too hot. It also brings cold water into the ocean, so the sea here is cool even on the warmest day.

cas-b-parus-na-doske.s: Next to surfing at Guincho, there is another kind of fun: windsurfing. It is a board with a mast and a sail. The sail is not fixed tight. You hold it by a bar with your hands and tilt it forwards, backwards and to the sides. That way you catch the wind and turn, like a cyclist with handlebars. On the waves the board bounces, and the windsurfer holds on and flies over the spray. Big competitions have even been held here.
a: You tilt it with your hands

cas-b-karavella.s: Many years ago, Portuguese sailors invented ships to sail off and discover new lands. They were called caravels. They were small and light, and their sails were triangular. Sails like that let a ship sail not only with the wind, but also a little against it. So caravels could travel far away and come back home. Today there are sailing boats in the ocean near Cascais too, only smaller.

cas-b-zigzag.s: The wind blows right in your face, and still the sailing boat moves forward! How? The sailors set the sail at an angle and go to the right, then to the left, in a zigzag, like a skier who climbs a hill in a “fir-tree” pattern. In the end, the boat gets where it needs to be. In the bay of Cascais you often see white sails, and from far away the boats look as if they are dancing. They are just catching the wind the way they need to.
a: In a zigzag, right then left

cas-b-probka-v-more.s: The Portuguese make cork from the bark of a special oak. It is as light as a feather and does not sink. The secret is that inside the cork there are millions of tiny cells full of air. So a piece of cork floats on water like a bobber. In the past, fishermen tied corks to their fishing nets so that the nets did not sink to the bottom. And cork is also used to make bottle stoppers, mats, bags and even hats.
a: It has lots of air inside
It is glued to the bottom

cas-b-probkovyj-dub.s: Cork oaks grow in the forests of Portugal. Once every nine years, their bark is carefully taken off, like a shirt. It does not hurt the tree. It just keeps growing and grows new bark. On the trunk that has just been stripped, people write the last number of the year in white paint. That way everyone knows when to expect the next harvest. The bare trunk is orange at first, and then it turns dark again.

cas-b-oblako-na-gore.s: Over the Sintra mountains there is often mist, even when the sun is shining in Cascais. Why is that? Damp air from the ocean runs up to the mountains, bumps into the slopes and rises up. Up there it cools, and clouds form from it. That is why the forests of Sintra are always damp and cool. Soft moss lies on the stones, and ferns grow between the trees, so it all looks like a fairy-tale jungle.
a: The mountains catch damp air from the ocean
Smoke comes out of a chimney

cas-b-evkalipt.s: If you walk over the hills near Cascais, you may suddenly smell something like cough sweets. That is the eucalyptus trees. They are not Portuguese. They were brought from faraway Australia. The trees grow fast and stretch up high, and their leaves are long and narrow and hang down. But there are no koalas in Portugal. They only eat the leaves of their own Australian eucalyptus trees, and they did not come here.

cas-b-sosny-zontiki.s: In the Sintra-Cascais park there are pine trees with a wide, flat top, like a sunshade. They are called stone pines. In their big cones there are little nuts, called pine nuts. The nuts ripen very slowly, in about three years! It is not easy to get them out of the cone, because the shell is hard. But in Portugal pine nuts are put into sweets and cakes. And in the heat it is nice to rest in the shade under such a pine.

cas-b-golubaya-soroka.s: In the pine and oak woods of Portugal lives a beautiful bird, the azure-winged magpie. It has a black cap, like a schoolchild, and its wings and long tail are a soft blue. They stay in noisy little flocks and call to each other loudly, like chatty friends. The most surprising thing is that a close relative of this bird lives in East Asia, thousands of kilometres away. Scientists are still talking about why it turned out like that.

cas-b-dyuny-dorozhki.s: Near Cascais, in the Cresmina dunes, there are wooden paths. They are there so that people do not walk on the sand and trample the plants. The sand does not blow away in the wind only because the roots of the grasses hold it. The roots are like an invisible net. If the grass is trampled, the wind blows the dune away. You walk on the boards, and on both sides little flowers bloom and lizards run by. It is beautiful, and nothing gets broken.

cas-b-volny-puteshestvenniki.s: The big waves at Cascais come from far away. Somewhere in the middle of the Atlantic, thousands of kilometres away, a stormy wind whips up the water. The waves run out from there and roll towards the shore for many days. When they reach Portugal, the storm is gone, but the waves are still there, smooth and long. Surfers love just that kind. You could say that every wave on the beach is a letter from the ocean.
a: From faraway storms in the ocean

cas-b-flagi-na-plyazhe.s: On the beaches of Portugal, little flags flutter. Green means you can swim. Yellow means it is better to go in only up to your knees. Red means you must not go in the water, because the waves are too big. Lifeguards watch the sea and change the flag in time. There is also a blue flag. It is given to beaches where the water is checked to be clean and where people take care of nature. If you see one, it means that people look after this place and the sea.
a: Clean water and care for nature
The beach is only for boats

cas-b-bola-de-berlin.s: A seller walks over the sand with a big basket and calls out, “Bolas de Berlim!” That is the name for round fried doughnuts. They are sprinkled with sugar, and inside hides a sweet egg cream. The name can be translated as “Berlin balls”, though they are baked all over Portugal. For children on the beach it is a real treat. Only, wipe your hands afterwards, or the sand will stick to the sugar and you will have to shake it off.

cas-b-travesseiro.s: In the little town of Sintra, near Cascais, bakers make flaky pastries called travesseiros. The word means “pillow”. The dough is rolled out very thin and folded like an envelope. Inside there is almond cream with egg, and outside there is sugar. It makes a crunchy little pillow that melts in your mouth. After a walk in the forests of Sintra, such a treat tastes extra good. Just don’t hurry: crumbs fall everywhere, and the pigeons are already waiting.

cas-b-kaldu-verdi.s: The Portuguese make a soup called “caldo verde”, which means “green broth”. It is made from potatoes and dark green kale. The kale is cut very, very thin, almost like threads, and dropped into the soup at the very end. Sometimes a thin slice of sausage goes on top, with a few drops of oil. It is served hot, with bread. It is good for warming up after the cool wind from the ocean.

cas-c-king-of-may.s: Umberto the Second was king of Italy for only a little more than a month, in the spring of 1946. That is why he was nicknamed the “May King”. Then he went to live in Portugal, in Cascais, and lived there for many years. A house was built for him and called “Villa Italia”. Today the house is a hotel, and tourists can stay in it, just as a real king once lived there.

cas-c-king-luis-shakespeare.s: King Luís the First loved music and books. He played the cello, and he also translated plays by the Englishman Shakespeare into Portuguese, for example “Hamlet”. The royal family spent the summer in Cascais, by the ocean. That is what this king was like: state business by day, and in the evening the cello and the words of a great writer, which he had to retell beautifully in Portuguese.

cas-c-king-carlos-painter.s: King Carlos the First loved not only to study the sea, but also to paint it. He painted pictures with paints, and he especially liked to draw the shore, boats and waves. His pictures were shown at exhibitions, and the king also studied the sea and the creatures that live in it, like a real scientist. The king spent the summers in Cascais and could paint what he saw from his window: the blue ocean, white sails and fishing boats by the shore.

cas-c-cable-telegram.s: In 1870, a long cable came ashore at Carcavelos, near Cascais. It lay on the bottom of the sea and joined Portugal to England. Telegrams ran along it: dots and dashes, faster than any ship. When the cable was opened, King Luís and the English Queen Victoria sent each other telegrams. After that, cables went on from Carcavelos out into the world.
a: On the bottom of the sea

cas-c-senna-estoril.s: Near Cascais, in Estoril, there is a racing track. In 1985 there was a heavy downpour there, but the Brazilian driver Ayrton Senna still came first and was more than a minute ahead of the others. It was his very first win in the big Formula 1 races. The track still works today: races are held there, and the ocean roars close by.

cas-c-game-macaca.s: Portuguese children play hopscotch, and the game is called “macaca”, which means “monkey”. They draw squares with numbers on the paving stones in chalk, throw a pebble and hop on one foot from square to square. They play in squares and on paths near the beach. The winner is the one who gets to the end and never steps on a line.

cas-c-game-piao.s: In Portugal, people love an old game with a wooden spinning top. It is called the “pião”. A child winds a string tightly round the top, throws it on the ground and pulls the end, and the top starts to spin! You can have a contest: whose top spins for longer. These toys are sold in little souvenir shops, and many grandmas and grandpas remember them from their childhood.

cas-c-berlin-balls.s: In summer, sellers with big baskets walk along the beaches and shout loudly, “Bolas de Berlim!” That is what the Portuguese call soft doughnuts sprinkled with sugar. The name means “Berlin balls”. The doughnut is cut open, and inside there is usually a sweet yellow cream. Children in Cascais love to eat them right on the sand, wiping the sugar off their noses.

cas-c-obrigado.s: In Portuguese, people say “thank you” in different ways, depending on who is speaking. A boy or a man says “obrigado”, and a girl or a woman says “obrigada”. The word changes a little at the end. So in a café in Cascais, this one word tells you at once whether you are talking to a boy or a girl. It is good that it is the most important word, and it is easy to learn.

cas-c-pao-por-deus.s: On the first of November in Portugal, children go from house to house with cloth bags and ask, “Pão por Deus!”, which means “bread for God’s sake”. The people at home put nuts, fruit, little buns and sweets into their bags. It is a very old custom. In some places children keep it up even today, and in the evening they have something to show their parents and count.

cas-c-sao-martinho.s: On the eleventh of November, Portugal celebrates Saint Martin’s Day. In the streets, people roast chestnuts and sell them hot in paper cones. Warm hands and the sweet smell of smoke: that is what children remember. At this time it is often as warm as summer, and the Portuguese even call it “Saint Martin’s summer”. You can eat chestnuts while you sit on a bench by the sea.

cas-c-june-sardines.s: In June, all over Portugal, and in Cascais too, there are festivals for the saints Anthony, John and Peter. In the streets people hang paper garlands, and in the yards they grill sardines over coals. A fresh little fish is put right on a slice of bread, and the juice soaks into the soft part. It is very tasty. Children run between the tables and wait for someone to give them a bite.

cas-c-manjerico.s: At the June festivals, the Portuguese give each other a “manjerico”, a small pot of sweet-smelling basil. A paper carnation is stuck into the soil, and a short poem is fixed to it: warm words or a joke. You do not eat the basil, you sniff it gently: it is enough to run your hand over the leaves, and the whole yard smells of it. Such a pot is put on the windowsill.

cas-c-bolo-rei.s: For Christmas, the Portuguese bake the “bolo-rei”, which means “king cake”. It is round, with a hole in the middle, like a crown, and covered with candied fruit and nuts. A broad bean is hidden in the dough, and in the past a little gift too. Whoever gets the bean must buy the same cake next year. So everyone eats carefully and looks into every slice.

cas-c-janeiras.s: At the start of January in Portugal, people go from house to house and sing New Year songs called “Janeiras”. It is an old custom. The people at home open the door, listen, and give the visitors sweets or something warm. Sometimes whole groups sing together: children, mums, grandpas. The songs are about a good year and about always having something to eat at home.

cas-c-festival-sea-procession.s: At the end of summer, Cascais has a festival of the sea. The main day is the fishermen’s procession. A statue of Our Lady of the Seafarers is carried to Ribeira beach and put on a fishing boat, and the dressed-up boats sail out to sea. People watch from the shore and wave, and on this day the fishermen are especially proud of their work. In 2023, this procession was named part of the country’s cultural heritage.

cas-c-name-shells.s: Nobody knows exactly where the town’s name comes from. There is one lovely version: it comes from the Portuguese word “cascas”, which means “shells”. Long ago, whole heaps of empty shells lay on the shore, and people named the place after them. It is nice to believe that it was so. Today you can find shells on the sand of Cascais yourself, and put them in your pocket to remember it by.

cas-c-bike-path.s: From the harbour of Cascais, a cycle path runs along the coast. It is about ten kilometres long and has almost no hills, so it is easy even for those who have only just learned to ride. On the way you can see cliffs, waves and seagulls, and at the end there is the big Guincho beach, where the wind always blows. You can hire a bike, and there are benches to rest on along the way.

cas-c-green-soup.s: One of the best-loved Portuguese soups is called “caldo verde”, which means “green soup”. It has potatoes, olive oil and a special cabbage that is cut into very, very thin ribbons, almost like threads. Sometimes a slice of sausage is put on top. Children and grown-ups both love this soup. It is served at festivals and at home, and in the evening, in a café in Cascais, it warms you up after the wind from the ocean.

cas-c-entrudo.s: Long ago, before Lent, Portugal celebrated “Entrudo”. People went out into the streets and had fun: they splashed water on each other, sprinkled flour and threw little bags. Nobody got angry: everyone was wet and laughing. Later this noisy festival became a calmer carnival, where children put on costumes and masks, and grown-ups decorate whole streets.
a: They splashed water and sprinkled flour

cas-c-folar.s: At Easter in Portugal, people bake “folar”, a sweet or salty bread with a surprise. A whole egg, still in its shell, is put into the dough, and a cross of dough is placed on top. The egg bakes together with the bread and turns hard. In some families, this bread is given to godchildren. Children happily look at the golden crust and try to find where the egg is hidden.

cas-c-st-anthony-fish.s: Saint Anthony was born in Lisbon, and the Portuguese love him very much. There is an old legend: when the people on the shore did not want to listen to him, he turned to the water and began to talk to the fish. The fish were said to have lifted their heads out of the water to listen. In June, on his day, there is a festival with garlands and treats, and the fishermen of Cascais remember this story with a smile.

cas-c-rooster-legend.s: In Portugal, painted roosters are sold: clay ones, wooden ones, ones on magnets. There is a legend behind them. A traveller was wrongly accused of stealing, and he said to the judge, “I am innocent, and here is the sign: this roast rooster on the table will crow.” The judge and his guests laughed, but the rooster jumped up and crowed! The traveller was set free. Since then the rooster has been a sign of luck and honesty.
a: It flew out of the window

cas-c-two-surnames.s: In Portugal, a person usually has not one surname but several. One comes from Mum, another from Dad, and sometimes there are more. So a full name can be very long. At school in Cascais, the teacher writes it down in full, and the children are proud that in their name live both Mum and Dad, and maybe Grandma and Grandpa too.

chn-a-stena-gory.s: The Great Wall of China does not lie in a straight line. It climbs over the mountain ridges like a long stone ribbon. Up, down and up again. In some places the steps are so steep that you have to hold the rail. The Wall was built of brick and stone, and in lands with no trees even of packed earth. Add up all its parts, ditches and natural barriers, and it is more than twenty thousand kilometres long. That is about halfway round the whole Earth!

chn-a-zapgorod-koshki.s: The Forbidden City is a museum now, and cats live there. Ginger, grey and patchy ones. People say there are more than a hundred and fifty. The museum workers call them guards: the cats catch mice that could nibble the old things. In the daytime the cats hide from the crowds, and they walk about mostly at night. The cats are looked after. They are fed and given medicine when they are ill.
a: They guard the gates from lions

chn-a-panda-malysh.s: A newborn panda is tiny and pink, with almost no fur. It weighs about a hundred grams, like a bar of chocolate. Its mum is hundreds of times heavier. For about a month the baby cannot see, because its eyes are closed. Mum holds it gently in her paw. But the baby grows fast, gets black and white fur and soon begins to crawl.
a: About as much as a chocolate bar
About as much as a big watermelon
About as much as a brick

chn-a-army-lica.s: Underground near the city of Xi’an stand thousands of clay soldiers. They are as tall as a person, or even taller. The makers shaped their faces, and almost no two are the same. One has a moustache, another a beard, a third a different hairstyle. Some soldiers look serious, and others seem to smile a little. Visitors walk along the rows and look for the kindest face.
a: Almost no two are the same

chn-a-shelk-tut.s: Silk is made by the silkworm caterpillar. It hatches from a tiny egg, very small. It eats only mulberry leaves, day after day. People say that when there are many caterpillars, their munching sounds like rain on leaves. In a month it grows dozens of times heavier and changes its skin four times. That is why people in China grew mulberry trees right next to the silk.

chn-b-newyear-envelope.s: At New Year in China, children are given red envelopes. Inside there is money, and kind words are printed on the envelope. The envelope is called a hongbao. Grown-up relatives give it and wish: grow big and healthy. You take the gift with both hands, as if it were something fragile, and politely say “thank you”. Usually you do not open the envelope in front of everyone.

chn-b-dragon-dance.s: At festivals a long dragon “crawls” along the streets of China. It is made of cloth and paper, and inside it, like in a train carriage, dozens of people walk. Each one holds a pole and lifts their own piece of the body. In front runs a person with a ball, like a pearl. The dragon plays and chases it. When everyone steps together, the dragon wiggles as if it were alive.

chn-b-guilin-cormorants.s: On the Li River you can sometimes see a fisherman on a long bamboo raft. Black birds called cormorants sit beside him. The bird dives and catches a fish, and the fisherman takes it. A thin little ring is put round the bird’s neck, so that it cannot swallow a big fish. The cormorant eats the small fish itself. This is a very old way of fishing: birds and people work together.

chn-b-tea-legend.s: An old legend tells of a ruler called Shennong. He liked to drink only boiled water. One day he sat under a tree while the water was boiling. The wind blew off a few little leaves, and they fell into the pot. The water turned golden and smelled lovely. The ruler took a sip and was surprised: the drink was pleasant and made him feel lively. That is how, says the legend, people found tea, a very long time ago.

chn-b-zodiac.s: In the Chinese calendar every year has its own animal. There are twelve: rat, ox, tiger, rabbit, dragon, snake, horse, goat, monkey, rooster, dog and pig. An old tale says they held a race across a river, and in one version it went like this. The clever rat climbed onto the ox’s back, jumped off at the finish and came first. That is why the year of the rat counts as the first. After twelve years the circle starts again.

chn-a-pekin-gnezdo.s: There is a stadium in Beijing that looks like a giant bird’s nest. It was built for the 2008 Olympic Games. The steel beams are woven together like twigs, and you can see the sky between them. From far away, it looks as if giant birds have built a nest. Tens of thousands of people can sit inside. No wonder it is called “the Bird’s Nest”.

chn-b-chopsticks-three-thousand.s: People in China have eaten with chopsticks for about three thousand years. At first, they say, chopsticks were used for cooking, to lift food out of a hot pot. Later they came to the table. They are made of bamboo or wood. Instead of a fork and knife, you hold two thin sticks. With some practice, you can pick up rice, noodles and even a tiny pea.

chn-b-lantern-festival.s: The New Year celebrations in China end with the Lantern Festival. It is on the fifteenth day of the new year. In the evening, the streets and parks glow with thousands of lanterns. They come in the shapes of fish, rabbits and dragons. Some lanterns have riddles written on them, and everyone wants to solve them. On this day people also eat sweet balls made of rice flour. They are called yuanxiao.

chn-b-shanghai-maglev.s: In Shanghai there is a train that does not touch the rails. It floats above the track on an invisible magnetic cushion. That is why it runs so smoothly and quietly. It used to speed up to almost 430 kilometres an hour, and today it goes a little slower. It travels the thirty kilometres to the airport in only eight minutes. Passengers barely have time to look at the city outside!

chn-b-terraces-yuanyang.s: In the south of China, the mountains look like giant staircases. These are the Yuanyang rice terraces. People carved the steps into the hillsides many hundreds of years ago. In spring the steps are filled with water, and each one shines like a mirror. The sky and the clouds are reflected in the water. Early in the morning, when there is mist over the mountains, it looks as if the staircase goes right up into the sky.

chn-b-noodles.s: On their birthday, people in China eat long noodles. They are called longevity noodles. One strand is made very long, and you try not to bite it through but to eat it whole. People say that the longer the noodle, the longer the life. It is just a fun and kind good-luck wish, and a tasty one. So on the party table the noodles are served uncut and long, and everyone wishes the birthday child good health.

chn-b-compass.s: People say that about two thousand years ago, the first thing like a compass was invented in China. It was described as a spoon made of a special stone, a magnet. It was placed on a smooth board, and it turned its handle to the south. Later came a needle that floated on water or hung on a thread. Sailors took it with them on voyages. That way the needle helped them not to get lost on the open sea.

chn-b-two-rivers.s: China has two very famous rivers. The Yangtze is the longest in Asia, more than six thousand kilometres. It flows through mountains and plains and runs into the sea near Shanghai. The Yellow River, in Chinese Huang He, is also very long. Its water is yellow because it carries a lot of sand and clay. Both rivers flow from west to east, and people have lived on their banks since ancient times.
a: It carries a lot of sand and clay

chn-a-bumaga-vyrezki.s: In China, people can cut real pictures out of paper. They take a red sheet, fold it in half or in four, and cut it with scissors. Unfold it, and a pattern appears: a flower, a fish, a little bird. The two halves are the same because the paper was folded. These paper cuttings are stuck on windows, and the light shines prettily through the red flowers.
a: The paper is folded in half
The pattern is drawn with a ruler
The paper is painted on both sides

chn-b-hieroglyph-pictures.s: A very long time ago, Chinese characters were just tiny pictures. A mountain was drawn with three sharp peaks. The sun was a little circle with a dot in the middle. A tree was drawn with a trunk, branches and roots. Over time the pictures became simpler and turned into strokes. But if you look closely, you can still see three peaks in the character for “mountain”!

es-holiday-grapes.s: On New Year’s Eve, people in Spain eat grapes. When the clock strikes twelve, you must eat twelve grapes, one for every bong. That is not easy, because you have to chew very fast! Each grape is said to bring good luck for one month of the new year. So before the party, shops sell grapes in little tins: twelve in each.

es-holiday-kings.s: In Spain, children get their presents from the Three Kings: Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar. On the evening of the fifth of January there is a parade, and the kings throw sweets into the crowd. Children leave their shoes by the door and put out water for the kings’ camels. On the morning of the sixth there are presents next to the shoes! With tea, people eat a round cake with a surprise inside: whoever finds the little king gets to wear a paper crown.

es-animals-lynx.s: In the south of Spain lives the Iberian lynx. It is a wild cat with a spotty coat, a short tail and little tassels on its ears, and fluffy whiskers on both sides of its face. It loves rabbits best of all. Not long ago there were very few of these lynxes left, but people started looking after them, and now there are more again. It is hard to spot one: the lynx is shy and likes to hide in the bushes.

es-food-churros.s: In Spain, people love churros for breakfast or a snack. They are long, golden sticks of dough fried in oil. You dip them in thick, warm chocolate, so thick that a spoon almost stands up in it. Churros are crunchy outside and soft inside. They are sold in little cafés, and sometimes at fairs, and children go home with chocolate moustaches.

es-segovia-aqueduct.s: In the middle of the streets of Segovia stands a Roman aqueduct. It was built almost two thousand years ago to bring water from the mountains to the town. It is about twenty-eight metres high and has more than a hundred and sixty arches. The most amazing thing is that the heavy granite stones sit on top of each other with no mortar or glue. Only their own weight holds them. And the aqueduct is still standing, strong and beautiful.
a: Only the weight of the stones

es-altamira-bison.s: In the north of Spain, in the Altamira cave, there are bison painted on the ceiling. They were painted by people in the Stone Age, a very, very long time ago, maybe more than fifteen thousand years ago. The artists used red and black paint and used the bumps in the rock, so the bison look round and solid. The paintings were first noticed by a little girl, the daughter of a man who was exploring the cave. Today an exact copy has been made next to it, so the real paintings are not spoiled.

es-bilbao-puppy.s: In front of the museum in Bilbao sits a giant puppy called Puppy. He is as tall as a four-storey house, about twelve metres. But the most amazing thing is that his “fur” is made of living flowers! Gardeners plant tens of thousands of plants in a metal frame, and inside are hidden pipes that water the puppy. In spring and summer he is bright and colourful, and every now and then the flowers are changed.
